OIL PIPELINEs GEOPOLITICS: Saudi Arabia has announced plans today to expand its key East-West pipeline (bypassing the Strait of Hormuz), which has a nominal capacity of 7m b/d (although currently is running probably at around 6m b/d after an attack destroyed a pumping station in September). 

In the next 7-8 weeks, Saudi Aramco would be able to boost capacity by 1.2m b/d using an existing natural gas pipe, making changes to ship crude. Riyadh didn't disclose further details, other than the line would need to revert to nat gas by May as the kingdom needs it to feed power stations during the summer months. 

[My hypothesis is this could be the old 48-inches, ~1,500-km long IPSA (Iraqi Pipeline in Saudi Arabia) built in the 1980s which runs largely parallel to the East-West pipeline from pumping station #3 all the way to near Yanbu. The pipeline was seized by the Saudis after Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in Aug 1990 and later it was repurposed for use in the country's Master Gas System]

More long-term, Saudi officials said they plan to boost shipping capacity of the East-West pipeline to ~10m b/d in the next 2-3 years, mostly improving pumping capacity (rather than building another pipe). 

For more on the East-West pipeline, I wrote this @Opinion column early on the conflict: https://t.co/4xlOFVnJxf

This is a short extract from my newsletter emailed to clients earlier today. If you would like to read my newsletters in full, three times a week, you can subscribe via my website https://t.co/aW1Xb1tAI9

At the end of September, I wrote that the market was incorrectly assuming that the Oman Lane flows would continue. Financial writers were so eager to proclaim that 1) Iran lost control and 2) oil flows are going back to normal. That turned out to be a very bad call.

The reality right now is that the Oman Lane transit flows continue. As of the latest figures I’ve seen, implied Strait of Hormuz flow is somewhere between 8 and 9 million b/d, down from 13-14 million b/d. The forward-looking implied flow (over the next 10 days) is expected to fall to 6-7 million b/d.

For the moment, oil traders continue to see the latest attacks as transitory. We are not seeing any material panic in the physical market just yet. The surge in crude volumes out of the Strait of Hormuz in mid-September is enough to calm things down a bit just as global refineries enter maintenance this time of the year, but I suspect elevated tanker rates are masking some of the inherent panic to come.

Furthermore, the diesel that may or may not reach the United States would most likely be shipped out of the Baltic terminal of Primorsk, which is over 2,000 km away from the Caspian Sea. Iranian diesel would most likely serve the needs of the Russian army right now since the refineries near Ukraine have been targeted repeatedly.
